title: Strongly Connected Components with Tarjan
excerpt: In a directed graph the useful grouping is not what you can reach but what can reach you back. One depth-first search and two numbers per node find every such group in linear time.
seoDescription: Tarjan's strongly connected components algorithm derived: why DFS puts each component in one contiguous subtree, what lowlink actually measures, why the stack distinguishes live cycles from finished components, and a full trace.

content.text: In an undirected graph, asking which nodes belong together is easy. Run one traversal, and everything it reaches is a connected component, because reachability goes both ways.
Directed graphs take that symmetry away. A one-way street from A to B tells you nothing about getting from B back to A. So the interesting grouping is no longer "can I reach it" but
"can we reach each other"
. A set of nodes where every node can reach every other node, and which cannot be made any bigger without breaking that, is a
strongly connected component

These matter more than they first appear. Mutually recursive functions form one in a call graph. Circular package dependencies form one in a build graph. Collapse each component to a single point and any directed graph becomes acyclic, which means you can then topologically sort it. Finding them is often the first step that makes a tangled graph tractable.

body.text: The obvious method, and its price

content.text: There is a direct way to compute this, and it is worth pricing before reaching for anything clever. For each node, run a traversal forwards to find everything it reaches, then run a traversal along reversed edges to find everything that reaches it, and intersect the two sets to get exactly the nodes mutually reachable with it, which is its component.
That is completely correct and costs two traversals per node, so
O(V * (V + E))

overall. On a graph with a hundred thousand nodes it is far too slow. The question is whether one pass can do it, and the answer turns out to be yes, using nothing but a depth-first search with two extra numbers per node.
Run a depth-first search on a directed graph and it carves the graph into a tree, the edges it actually descended through, plus leftover edges that point to nodes already discovered.
Now here is the fact that makes a one-pass algorithm possible. Every strongly connected component appears in that DFS tree as a
contiguous block
. All its nodes sit in one subtree, and exactly one of them was discovered first. Call that node the component's
root

The reason is not hard to see. If two nodes are mutually reachable and DFS enters one of them, it can reach the other before it leaves, so the other is discovered somewhere below it. So a component never gets split across unrelated parts of the tree.

That reduces the whole problem to a single question. If you can recognize, at the moment DFS finishes with a node, whether that node is the root of a component, then everything discovered since you entered it and not yet claimed must be its component. Recognizing roots is the entire algorithm.

Give every node a discovery number as you enter it: 0 for the first node entered, 1 for the next, and so on. Call it index, and once a node has one it keeps it for the rest of the run, since nothing revisits a node to renumber it.
Then give every node a second number called
low
, which answers this question:
what is the smallest index I can reach, going down through my subtree and then taking at most one edge back up?
A node starts with
low
equal to its own
index
, because it can certainly reach itself. It then improves in two ways. When you return from a child, your
low
takes the minimum of itself and the child's
low
, since anything the child can climb to, you can climb to through the child. And when you see an edge to a node that was already discovered and is still in play, your
low
takes the minimum of itself and that node's
index
Now the payoff. If a node finishes with
low
strictly less than its
index
, something in its subtree found a way back to an ancestor. That ancestor and this node are on a cycle together, so they share a component, and this node cannot be the first one entered in it.
If a node finishes with
low
equal to its
index
, nothing beneath it escaped upward. Nothing in its subtree can reach anything discovered before it. That is exactly what being the first node of a component means.
low equals index identifies a root
, and everything still unclaimed below it is its component.

body.text: Why there is a stack, and the subtlety inside it

content.text: Keep a stack of every node discovered but not yet assigned to a finished component. Push a node when you enter it. When a root finishes, pop until you pop the root itself, and those nodes are the component.
That much is bookkeeping. The stack is also doing something less obvious, and this is the one part of Tarjan's algorithm that genuinely catches people out.
When DFS meets an edge to a node that has already been discovered, there are two very different situations, and they need opposite treatment.

rows: A node still on the stack
It is an ancestor or a node in the same unfinished region, so it can reach back to you
Update low using that node's index
It sits in a finished component, which by definition cannot reach back to you

content.text: Miss that second case and components start merging that have no business merging. The edge exists, so you can get there, but there is no route back, and a component needs both directions.
One more detail in the same area. When you take an edge to a node on the stack, you use that node's
index
and not its
low
. Using
low
can pull in a value from a region that cannot actually reach you, which merges components that should stay apart. The version with
index
is the one that is correct, and it is a common source of a solver that works on small tests and fails on larger ones.
Here is a graph with four components of different shapes: one cycle of three, one cycle of two, and two single nodes.
Starting the DFS at A, with neighbors taken in the order listed. Step through it below and watch the low values travel back up as the recursion unwinds.
Four things in that trace are worth going back to. C reached A, an ancestor, so C's
low
dropped to 0 and that 0 propagated up through B to A. D had a child, E, whose component finished underneath it, and D's own
low
was untouched by it, which is exactly right: E's component cannot get back to D.

Also notice the order components come out. E and F finished first, then G, then D, then the big one containing A. Tarjan produces components in reverse topological order of the collapsed graph, which is a free bonus. If you need that order the right way round, reverse the output rather than sorting it.

And notice that A, the very first node entered, was a root with low 0 equal to its index 0, since the first node of a DFS is always a root of something, because nothing was discovered before it for anything to climb back to.

The panel shows each node's index and low as they change. Watch for the moment a low value drops because of a back edge, then watch that value climb the recursion. The components get outlined as they are popped.
Every node is entered once and pushed once. Every edge is examined once, from its tail. Each node is popped at most once. Add those up and the whole thing is
O(V + E)
, the same as a plain DFS, which is the point of the exercise: it beats the two-traversals-per-node approach by a whole factor of V.
Memory is
O(V)

for the two number arrays, the stack, and the on-stack flags. The recursion depth can reach V on a long chain, which is the same stack overflow risk any recursive DFS carries, and the same fix applies if you hit it.
Using low instead of index for an edge to a stacked node.
The single most common error, and a nasty one because small graphs often give the right answer anyway. Components come out merged that should be separate.
Updating low from a node that is already off the stack.
Same symptom, different cause. A finished component cannot reach you, so an edge into one carries no information about cycles and must be skipped entirely.
Only running the DFS from one node.

A directed graph is very often not reachable from any single starting point. Loop over every node and start a fresh DFS from any that is still undiscovered, exactly as with counting connected components.
Expecting components in topological order.
They come out reversed. That is useful once you know it and a confusing off-by-everything bug until you do.
Forgetting that a single node is a component.

A node on no cycle at all forms a component of size one. In the trace above, D and G are each their own component. Code that only records components of two or more will silently drop most of the graph.
Short, considering what it does, and the two comment lines are where all the difficulty was.

variants.code:
def tarjan(graph):
    index, low, on_stack = {}, {}, set()
    stack, components = [], []
    counter = 0

    def visit(v):
        nonlocal counter
        index[v] = low[v] = counter
        counter += 1
        stack.append(v)
        on_stack.add(v)

        for w in graph.neighbors(v):
            if w not in index:
                visit(w)                     # tree edge
                low[v] = min(low[v], low[w])
            elif w in on_stack:
                # w can still reach back to v. Use its INDEX, not its low.
                low[v] = min(low[v], index[w])
            # w visited but off the stack: finished component, ignore it

        if low[v] == index[v]:               # v is a root
            component = []
            while True:
                w = stack.pop()
                on_stack.discard(w)
                component.append(w)
                if w == v:
                    break
            components.append(component)

    for v in graph.nodes:
        if v not in index:
            visit(v)
    return components

questions.prompt: A node finishes with low equal to its index. What does that tell you?

options.label: It is the root of a component, and everything above it on the stack belongs to that component

questions.prompt: DFS finds an edge to a node that was visited but is no longer on the stack. What should happen?

options.label: Nothing. That node is in a finished component that cannot reach back
Update low using that node's index
Update low using that node's low

questions.prompt: Why use the neighbor's index rather than its low when it is on the stack?

options.label: Its low may come from a region that cannot reach you, which would merge separate components
Its low has not been computed yet at that point
The two are always equal for stacked nodes

questions.prompt: In what order does Tarjan output the components?

options.label: Reverse topological order of the graph you get by collapsing each component to a point
The order their roots were discovered

questions.prompt: Why is this better than running a forward and a backward traversal from every node?

options.label: It answers the same question in one DFS, so O(V + E) instead of O(V * (V + E))
It handles graphs with cycles, which traversals cannot
It needs no extra memory beyond the graph
